uncited: Hardware-Assisted Projection is a family of volume rendering techniques that offload the computationally intensive tasks of projection, scan conversion, and compositing to the graphics processing unit (GPU).

It solves the performance bottlenecks of CPU-based projected tetrahedra by leveraging the parallel architecture of modern graphics hardware to achieve interactive rendering rates [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

Unlike traditional raycasting, which operates in image space, these methods maintain the object-order nature of projected tetrahedra but utilize hardware pipelines for rasterization and fragment processing, often eliminating the need for explicit CPU-side sorting or triangle generation [S2, unofficial].
All methods in this family share the core principle of mapping 3D unstructured grid elements (tetrahedra or polyhedra) to 2D screen space using the graphics pipeline.
**Projection:** Transforming 3D vertices to screen coordinates using view and projection matrices.
**Scan Conversion:** Rasterizing the projected elements into fragments.
This may involve generating triangles (as in standard PT) or processing point primitives that are decomposed into triangles by a geometry shader.
**Volume Integration:** Computing the volume ray integral within the fragment shader, often using partial pre-integration techniques to handle opacity and color accumulation accurately.
**Compositing:** Accumulating the color and opacity of fragments, typically using front-to-back alpha blending.
*   **GPU-Centric Pipeline:** The rendering logic is implemented in vertex, geometry, and fragment shaders, minimizing data transfer between CPU and GPU [S2, unofficial].
*   **No Explicit Pre-processing:** Unlike some CPU-based approaches, these methods often require no pre-processing of the mesh data beyond loading it into GPU memory [S1, unofficial].
*   **Depth Sorting:** Accurate compositing requires depth sorting.

This is achieved either by pre-sorting the elements on the CPU/GPU before rendering [S2, unofficial] or by using hardware depth buffering and blending operations if the sorting is implicit or approximate.
The family originates from the need to accelerate the Projected Tetrahedra (PT) algorithm, which was originally designed for CPU rendering [Parent](877-projected-tetrahedra.md).
As GPU capabilities advanced, researchers adapted PT to leverage hardware acceleration.

Key developments include the use of geometry shaders for dynamic triangle generation [S2, unofficial] and the application of partial pre-integration in fragment shaders for accurate volume rendering [S2, unofficial].

The methods are widely used in interactive visualization of unstructured grids, such as in finite element analysis and medical imaging, where large datasets require real-time feedback [S1, unofficial].
